title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Sensing
authors: Lorcan O. Conlon, Yu-Xin Wang, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Victor V. Albert, Michael J. Gullans, Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract: Quantum sensors hold great promise for achieving better sensitivity in the measurement of physical quantities compared to their classical counterparts. However, the conditions under which quantum advantage in sensing can be achieved are rather restrictive, and most quantum enhancements in sensing are lost in the presence of noise, errors, or a poorly calibrated system. To overcome these limitations, we are motivated to import ideas from fault-tolerant quantum computing to quantum sensing. Specifically, we consider a qubit noise model where the probability of phase-flip errors is exponentially smaller (in qubit number) compared to the probability of bit-flip errors that occur with probability $p$. For this noise structure, we demonstrate that, given a total sensing time $T$, Heisenberg scaling can be attained for times up to $T\propto 1/p^{(N+1)/2}$ for a $N$-qubit repetition code, in contrast with $T\propto 1/p$ without using a fault-tolerant sensing protocol.
summary: This paper addresses the fragility of high-precision quantum sensing in the presence of noise by importing fault-tolerance concepts from quantum computing. It demonstrates that under a specific restricted error model, Heisenberg scaling—the ultimate sensitivity limit—can be maintained for extended sensing times using simple repetition codes. This shows a pathway to robust quantum measurements beyond current theoretical limitations.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving quantum advantage in sensing by reaching the Heisenberg limit while mitigating noise effects that typically degrade entanglement-enhanced protocols.
main_result: Under a restricted qubit noise model, the authors demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling can be maintained for sensing times up to $T\propto 1/p^{(N+1)/2}$ using a simple repetition code, surpassing the naive error scaling.
method: The work adapts concepts from fault-tolerant quantum computing (QEC) to metrology, analyzing how specific noise structures allow for the restoration of Heisenberg scaling through encoding and recovery operations.
model_or_system: The system involves $N$ qubits used as sensors estimating a phase $\phi$. The analysis compares ideal sensing limits (SQL vs. HL) against noisy evolution governed by error probabilities ($p$) and utilizes repetition codes derived from QEC theory.
key_observables: Estimation error ($\sigma_\phi$), Visibility, Fisher Information (CFI/QFI), and the scaling of achievable time $T$.
important_parameters: Error probability $p$, number of qubits $N$, sensing time $T$, and the structure of the noise model.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a specific, restricted qubit noise model where phase-flip errors are exponentially smaller than bit-flip errors. It also assumes the applicability of fault-tolerance ideas derived from quantum computing.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates three sensing protocols: separable ($\sigma_\phi \propto 1/\sqrt{N}$), entangled ($\sigma_\phi \propto 1/N$), and sequential uses ($\sigma_\phi \propto 1/N$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical limits of quantum sensing (SQL vs. HL) to identifying how noise degrades these enhancements, culminating in proposing fault-tolerance techniques derived from quantum computing to restore Heisenberg scaling under specific error assumptions.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges two major fields: quantum metrology and quantum error correction. For AMO physicists studying open quantum systems, it provides a concrete theoretical framework for how robust sensing protocols can be engineered using QEC principles against realistic noise channels.
